title: Paddy's Has a Jumper

jokes.text: Characters are deeply engrossed in a British period drama, rhapsodizing about how much they love it despite one admitting they 'usually hate this old-time British crap'
jokes.setup: These are four selfish, lowbrow characters who are introduced watching a sentimental British period romance with genuine emotional investment
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of these awful people being completely swept up in a prestige romance they'd normally mock establishes the episode's ironic baseline
jokes.explanation: A solid cold-open joke that sets up the episode's theme: the gang outsourcing their decision-making. The irony is good but doesn't have a sharp punchline — it's more of a sustained tone-setter.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: If you'll have me as your husband, that is what you shall be.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Whoa! What? Oh, my God. I did not see that coming.

jokes.text: "The algorithm, it takes thinking out of the equation, basically." / "Well, that's because math and computers can think better for us than we can think for ourselves."
jokes.setup: Dennis explains how the streaming algorithm predicts what shows they'll love
jokes.punchline: Mac enthusiastically agrees that outsourcing all cognitive function to a computer is desirable — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Seeds the episode's central satirical theme efficiently. The joke works because it perfectly characterizes these people as intellectually lazy and self-unaware. Gets a rewatch bonus because it pays off repeatedly through the algorithm bit.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I usually hate this old-time British crap... But, like, this-this show is amazing.

jokes.text: "Yeah... ooh, shut up, shut up. I-It's decided we're watching another one." / "Ah, I love that it does that, too. Another thing I don't have to think about."
jokes.setup: They're praising the algorithm for predicting their tastes
jokes.punchline: Dennis celebrates autoplay as 'another thing I don't have to think about' — framing cognitive autonomy as a burden to be shed
jokes.explanation: Economical reinforcement of the theme. Funny but slight — it's the third beat on the same joke, so diminishing returns set in.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: The algorithm... all of our previously-watched shows, they go into a data bank, so they can accurately predict which shows you'll love

jokes.text: "Cop! Cop!" — the gang panics at the sight of a police officer entering the bar even though they've done nothing wrong in this moment
jokes.setup: The gang is relaxed watching TV; a police officer enters
jokes.punchline: Instant, reflexive panic from all four — a perfect character beat revealing their baseline guilt complex
jokes.explanation: Two words that perfectly encapsulate who these characters are. The economy is exceptional — no setup needed, the panic IS the joke. It's deeply character-integrated because it only works for people with this much suppressed criminal guilt. Strong moment.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Math and computers can think better for us than we can think for ourselves

jokes.text: "We have nothing to do with that!" — the gang immediately and reflexively denies involvement in the suicide before anyone has suggested they're involved
jokes.setup: Officer says there's a suicidal man on the roof
jokes.punchline: Dennis's immediate denial of culpability before any accusation is made — classic guilty conscience
jokes.explanation: Economical character joke. The preemptive denial says everything about Dennis and the gang's relationship with authority. Pairs well with the cop panic moment for a one-two character comedy punch.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: When you watch stuff like this, you feel like you want to eat like the British

jokes.text: "Thank you for your service. Yeah, we love, we love the police. Blue-Blue Lives Matter, Blue Lives Matter."
jokes.setup: Gang was just panicking about the cop; officer is now leaving
jokes.punchline: They immediately pivot to performative pro-cop flattery the moment they're no longer under suspicion — total sycophantic hypocrisy
jokes.explanation: Decent beat that extends the cop-panic joke. The 'Blue Lives Matter' invocation is a nice contemporary touch that feels authentic to these characters' shallow politics. Slightly bloated delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Cop! Cop! I'm filming this! I didn't do it...

jokes.text: "You guys know what this means, right?" / "We're not gonna get our fish and chips."
jokes.setup: A man is suicidal on their roof and they're locked in; the moment calls for some acknowledgment of the gravity
jokes.punchline: Charlie's only concern is the fish and chips delivery being disrupted — the punchline arrives after a beat of genuine expectation that something meaningful will be said
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: the setup creates genuine anticipation that someone will process the gravity of the situation, then Charlie completely deflates it with the most trivial possible concern. The fish and chips has been mentioned once before, making this earned. Economy is excellent — it's exactly the right length. This is classic Always Sunny character comedy at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We have nothing to do with that!

jokes.text: "Bryan O'Brien." / "I'd kill myself, too, if I had that clown's name."
jokes.setup: News broadcast reveals the jumper's name: Bryan O'Brien
jokes.punchline: Mac's immediate reaction is that the rhyming clown name is itself sufficient reason for suicide — dark, quick, and unexpectedly logical
jokes.explanation: Sharp, dark, perfectly timed. The name 'Bryan O'Brien' is itself a comedic gift and Mac's response is the exactly right take on it. Very quotable. The structure is clean: name is revealed, brief pause, devastating non-sequitur judgment. Gets slightly docked on character integration because anyone could say this, but it also sets up the callback about Mac's own clown name.

dialogue.line: Thank you for your service. We love the police. Go blue. Blue Lives Matter.

jokes.text: "You literally have the name of a clown."
jokes.setup: Mac mocks Bryan O'Brien's rhyming name
jokes.punchline: Dennis immediately points out that Mac Ronald McDonald is himself named after a clown — instant comeuppance
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy joke. Five words that devastate Mac's moral high ground. The callback to Mac's series-long clown name is deeply character-integrated — it only works because of established lore. The structure is impeccable: Mac sets the trap, Dennis springs it. One of the episode's best lines by sheer efficiency-to-impact ratio.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We're not gonna get our fish and chips.

jokes.text: "All right, you know what? This is moving a little too slow for me. Let's-let's-let's click it back over to the show, yeah?"
jokes.setup: News coverage of a potential suicide is unfolding live
jokes.punchline: Dennis wants to change back to the British drama because the real suicide is 'moving too slow' — treating a man's potential death with the impatience of a bored TV viewer
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy beat. Dennis applying entertainment-consumer logic to a crisis is a sharp character moment. It also sets up the TV-watching-vs-crisis thread that runs through the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Bryan O'Brien. I'd kill myself, too, if I had that clown's name.

jokes.text: "He'd go 'down the road' instead of 'across the street.'" — Mac using colloquial euphemisms for the correct vs. incorrect way to slit a wrist, then being confused that no one understands him
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to explain that the jumper isn't serious, using a wrist-slitting metaphor
jokes.punchline: His use of casual street-direction euphemisms for a detailed self-harm technique, delivered as if this is common knowledge, is deeply absurd
jokes.explanation: The euphemisms are clever — the joke works on two levels: Mac's breezy familiarity with the topic and his confusion that others don't share his baseline knowledge. 'Across the street' vs. 'down the road' has genuine wit.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You literally have the name of a clown.

jokes.text: Mac describes in clinical detail the 'proper way' to slit one's wrist — 'from metacarpal straight to bicep, connecting with the artery the entire time' — and everyone's horrified reaction is at Dee, not Mac
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to prove the jumper isn't serious by saying someone who really wanted to die would use a bath
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers genuinely expert knowledge of self-harm method with disturbing clinical precision, then everyone acts like Dee's knowledge of it is the disturbing part
jokes.explanation: Layered dark comedy. First Mac displays weirdly specific self-harm knowledge, then the punchline is displaced onto Dee — the group uses her as a scapegoat to avoid confronting Mac's equally disturbing knowledge. Classic Always Sunny moral dodge.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: If the guy actually wanted to off himself, he'd hop into a warm bath and he'd do the old... north, south. Down the road instead of across the street.

jokes.text: "I am an American! I can believe in whatever I want in any given moment based on what argument I'm trying to make."
jokes.setup: Charlie catches Mac praising algorithms/science for TV but rejecting science when it comes to the jumper's survival odds
jokes.punchline: Mac's defense of his inconsistency is a perfect satire of motivated reasoning dressed up as patriotism
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. It's a sharp piece of political/cultural satire embedded in character comedy — Mac is articulating, with perfect clarity and total lack of self-awareness, the actual logical structure of motivated reasoning. 'I am an American' as the justification for selective epistemology is both funny and genuinely biting. Highly quotable, deeply character-integrated, earned. This approaches the 8.0 anchor in quality.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: The proper way to slit your wrist is take a knife and go from metacarpal straight to bicep, connecting with the artery the entire time.

jokes.text: "You are not a true American, Charlie." / "I'm more American than you will ever be!"
jokes.setup: Mac invokes patriotism to justify logical inconsistency
jokes.punchline: The argument immediately escalates into a meaningless American-ness competition that has nothing to do with the original point
jokes.explanation: Decent escalation beat that extends the joke but doesn't add much new. The playground escalation of 'I'm more American than you' is predictable, though it fits these characters.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm not talking... we're not talking about me. We're talking about him.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Are we not? I think we're...

jokes.text: "What we need is an algorithm." — Dennis's solution to an emotional argument about a suicidal person is to build an algorithm
jokes.setup: Dennis tells everyone to calm down and says he has a way to solve the argument without emotion
jokes.punchline: The 'solution' is to apply the same streaming algorithm logic to whether a human being should live or die
jokes.explanation: The pivot of the episode. Dennis applying Netflix-style algorithmic logic to a human life is the central satirical joke, and this is the moment it crystallizes. The callback structure is clean and earned — the opening scene perfectly set this up. Character-integrated because Dennis's controlling, systematizing personality makes this feel inevitable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He's not gonna die falling from that height.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Hard disagree, pal. You could absolutely die.

jokes.text: "This is my Behavioral Predictor algorithm" — Dennis's whiteboard algorithm has three questions: 'Could he?', 'Would he?', 'Should we?'
jokes.setup: Dennis presents his algorithm for deciding whether to intervene in a suicide
jokes.punchline: The 'algorithm' is literally just three vague questions on a whiteboard — a parody of data-driven decision-making that is entirely circular
jokes.explanation: Good visual gag that the audience can infer from the script — the elaborate buildup to what is clearly a comically simple whiteboard. Dennis's confidence in this obvious non-algorithm is the joke. Works within the episode's satirical frame.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I am an American! I can believe in whatever I want in any given moment based on what argument I'm trying to make.

jokes.text: "Uh, luckily I brought an egg to work today." — Charlie produces an egg from his pocket to use as a human-head proxy in a physics test
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Charlie to demonstrate if the jumper could die from the fall height
jokes.punchline: Charlie, characteristically, happens to have brought a random egg to work, treating this as a perfectly normal thing to do
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Charlie. The fact that he has an egg on him at all is the joke — no explanation, no apology, just matter-of-fact. The egg test itself as a scientific methodology for predicting fatal fall outcomes is good absurdism. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You are not a true American, Charlie. I'm more American than you will ever be!

jokes.text: Charlie enacts the egg drop with a miniature Paddy's Pub model while doing a voice: "Oh, I feel so sad. Life is so..." before dropping it
jokes.setup: Charlie is performing a 'scientific' test using an egg and a cardboard model of Paddy's Pub
jokes.punchline: He gives the egg a little suicidal monologue before dropping it, adding absurdist character work to what was already an absurd experiment
jokes.explanation: Charming absurdist moment. Charlie's earnestness is always the key ingredient. The miniature Paddy's model is a great visual detail that elevates what could be a simple egg drop joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What we need is an algorithm.

jokes.text: "Well, I don't think he's sad, I think he's happy to get off this merry-go-round." — Dee answering a question about what the suicidal egg-character would say
jokes.setup: Charlie asks Dee what the suicidal person would say in this situation, expecting a generic answer
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately has an oddly specific, resigned take — 'happy to get off this merry-go-round' — that reveals she's thought about this personally
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dee jokes in the episode. The phrase 'happy to get off this merry-go-round' is specific, poetic, and immediately tells you she's not talking about the egg. The horror of the group's reaction ('That's so pathetic. I'd never...') while completely missing that Mac just gave identical information is a good layered joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: My Behavioral Predictor algorithm... Could he? Would he? Should we?

jokes.text: "Oh, my God. That's so pathetic. I'd never... I would never..." / "You've thought about it. You had that in the chamber."
jokes.setup: Dee's specific answer about being 'happy to get off the merry-go-round' implies personal experience
jokes.punchline: The group piles on Dee while completely ignoring that Mac himself just demonstrated equivalent knowledge moments before
jokes.explanation: 'You had that in the chamber' is a sharp line. The group's selective moral outrage directed at Dee is classic Always Sunny dynamics — she's always the designated scapegoat.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Luckily I brought an egg to work today.

jokes.text: "If I'm being honest, I was hoping his entire skull would just explode." / "Right. I think we all were, Mac. We were hoping for a bit of an explosion."
jokes.setup: The egg breaks with underwhelming results after the drop test
jokes.punchline: Mac admits genuine disappointment that there wasn't more gore, and Dennis validates this as a universal feeling — the group's bloodlust is normalized
jokes.explanation: Dennis's calm validation — 'I think we all were' — is funnier than Mac's admission. The collective bloodlust framed as a universal, reasonable feeling is good dark comedy. Fits Dennis's sociopathic tendencies perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What would you say in this situation?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I don't think he's sad, I think he's happy to get off this merry-go-round.

jokes.text: "No. Unfortunately, that was the only one I found." / "Found? What does that mean?"
jokes.setup: Dennis asks if Charlie has an uncooked egg for a more accurate test
jokes.punchline: Charlie says the hard-boiled one was the only one he 'found' — implying he sourced it from a wild nest, not a store
jokes.explanation: The word 'found' doing enormous comedic work. It recontextualizes the entire egg, and Dee's immediate alarm at the phrasing is the perfect reaction. Very Charlie — he doesn't see anything wrong with foraging eggs.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You had that in the chamber.

jokes.text: "Goddamn it, Dee, are you eating my egg?" / "Well, yeah. I got hungry." / "You bitch. That was the only one in the nest."
jokes.setup: Dee has eaten the hard-boiled egg they needed for a second test
jokes.punchline: Charlie's outrage at Dee eating 'the only one in the nest' — confirming it was indeed a wild egg — lands with escalating absurdity
jokes.explanation: 'That was the only one in the nest' is a great escalation of the previous beat. Charlie's genuine outrage about losing a foraged wild egg is funny. Dee's total nonchalance ('I got hungry') is perfect counterpoint — she ate a nest egg and can't see why that's a problem.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I was hoping his entire skull would just explode. We all were, Mac.

jokes.text: "Well, it wasn't in a tree, it was in a hole." / "Yeah. I mean, it's like a rat's egg or something."
jokes.setup: Everyone's horrified that Charlie stole eggs from a nest
jokes.punchline: Charlie clarifies the egg was in a hole, not a tree, and speculates it's 'a rat's egg or something' — rats don't lay eggs, Charlie doesn't know this
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'A rat's egg or something' is perfect Charlie — he has no basic zoological knowledge, is totally unfazed, and treats this as a reasonable answer. The specificity ('not in a tree, it was in a hole') makes it funnier. Rats don't lay eggs is the unspoken punchline the audience fills in. High originality, extraordinary character integration. Genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It wasn't in a tree, it was in a hole. It's, like, a rat's egg or something.

jokes.text: "Oh, you know what, I might be able to get Frank's secret casaba melon." / "Why does Frank keep a casaba melon in the safe?"
jokes.setup: They need something to represent a human head; Charlie suggests Frank's secret melon
jokes.punchline: The existence of a 'secret casaba melon' kept in a safe immediately implies something deeply weird is going on, which the group immediately recognizes
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the melon payoff later. The specificity of 'casaba' melon is funny, and 'in the safe' does the heavy lifting. The group's immediate suspicion is well-earned.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Frank's secret casaba melon...

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Why does Frank keep a casaba melon in the safe?

jokes.text: "Has he cut a hole in the rind, and then put it back on, like a plug?" — Mac's immediate hypothesis about the melon
jokes.setup: The group speculates why Frank keeps a casaba melon locked in a safe
jokes.punchline: Mac's question is so specific — a hole with a 'plug' rind replacement — that it implies disturbing knowledge of exactly what Frank would do
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Mac's hypothesis — 'a plug' — is what makes this funny. It suggests Mac has thought about this previously or has knowledge of Frank's methods. Good dark comedy with strong character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Has he cut a hole in the rind, and then put it back on, like a plug?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah.

jokes.text: "You guys think he's having sex with it?" / "Well... yeah." / "He's definitely having sex with it."
jokes.setup: The group has been dancing around the implication
jokes.punchline: Dennis says the quiet part loud; everyone immediately agrees with total certainty — no hesitation
jokes.explanation: The punchline is obvious — which is partly the joke, since the whole group was clearly thinking it. The unanimity is funny but the beat is a bit easy. Frank being a sexual deviant is well-established series territory, so this doesn't feel fully fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Stay away from my stuff. Don't put your hands near my casaba.

jokes.text: "Stay away from my stuff. Don't put your hands near my casaba."
jokes.setup: Frank arrives and they tell him they need his casaba melon
jokes.punchline: Frank's specific territorial language about the melon — 'my casaba' — without any self-awareness about how this sounds
jokes.explanation: Frank's total lack of self-awareness is the joke. 'Don't put your hands near my casaba' lands as an inadvertent double entendre given the context. Decent but the joke has already been established.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You don't understand. It's my son.

jokes.text: "You-you banging it?" / "It's none of your goddamn business, Dennis. None of your goddamn business!" / "Banging it. Yeah."
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Frank directly if he's having sex with the melon
jokes.punchline: Frank's explosive non-denial — 'None of your goddamn business!' rather than 'No, that's disgusting' — is a perfect non-answer that answers everything
jokes.explanation: Frank's refusal to deny it is funnier than any admission would be. 'None of your goddamn business' as applied to melon-sex is a great character beat. Mac's quiet 'Banging it. Yeah.' as a verdict is a perfect deadpan button.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Cricket! Where did you come from?

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: I was up on the roof getting eggs from a nest.

jokes.text: "Dennis is touching my melon." — Frank's complaint to the police officer who has just walked in
jokes.setup: Frank tries to get to the safe; Dennis physically blocks him
jokes.punchline: Frank's complaint to a police officer — 'Dennis is touching my melon' — in the context of the established melon-sex suspicion makes this an accidental double entendre delivered completely straight
jokes.explanation: 'Dennis is touching my melon' is extremely economical and funny in context. Frank's obliviousness is total — he doesn't hear the double entendre even as the audience does. Good callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: I've fallen off buildings before; I never die. And look at me. I'm doing great.

jokes.text: "Cricket! Where did you come from?" / "I was up on the roof getting eggs from a nest."
jokes.setup: The gang is about to drop the melon when Cricket appears seemingly out of nowhere
jokes.punchline: Cricket has also been foraging eggs from a nest — tying him to Charlie's earlier egg subplot in a perfect absurdist convergence
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke. Cricket's unexpected entrance with his own egg-foraging mission perfectly mirrors Charlie's earlier behavior and suggests these two exist on the same feral social register. The 'I was up on the roof getting eggs' line is both a logical explanation and deeply absurd. Cricket's appearances always work best when they're earned by plot logic, and this one is.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're sort of subhuman at this point.

jokes.text: "Yeah, but you're not really a trustworthy control group, Cricket. I mean, you know, you're sort of subhuman at this point."
jokes.setup: Cricket volunteers himself as evidence that falling from buildings isn't fatal ('I've fallen off buildings before; I never die')
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses Cricket as a control group not because his sample size is too small, but because he is 'subhuman' — using scientific language to insult Cricket's dehumanized status
jokes.explanation: Good Cricket joke. The twist of using scientific language ('control group') to frame cruelty is consistent with the episode's algorithm satire. Cricket's degraded status being stated as matter-of-fact scientific fact is dark and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Maureen Ponderosa. She died from falling off a much shorter building.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, but you pushed her.

jokes.text: "I don't know how to squeeze that one into the algorithm."
jokes.setup: Cricket claims to be living proof falling from buildings isn't fatal
jokes.punchline: Mac's concern isn't that Cricket might be right or wrong, but that his data point doesn't fit the algorithm's format
jokes.explanation: Nice economical joke that continues the algorithm satire and characterizes Mac as genuinely trying to do the work. The idea that Cricket is an outlier who breaks the data model is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, no, no, they never proved that. That was never even proven that she was pushed.

jokes.text: "I've fallen off buildings before; I never die. And look at me. I'm doing great."
jokes.setup: The gang is debating whether someone could die from falling off the roof
jokes.punchline: Cricket, visibly destroyed by years of abuse, presents himself as evidence that falling off buildings is survivable — while being a walking argument that survival isn't always better than death
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Look at me. I'm doing great.' from Cricket — a man physically ruined by years of the gang's abuse — is perfect dark comedy. The line only works because the audience knows Cricket's history. The delivery of 'I'm doing great' as genuine self-assessment from someone clearly not doing great is devastatingly funny. Exceptional character integration; this joke exists nowhere else in television.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Just go through their trash. Sleep with them. Talk to their priest, then sleep with their priest. Then blackmail the priest.

jokes.text: "Maureen Ponderosa. Now, she died from falling off a much shorter building." / "Yeah, but you pushed her." / "No, no, no... they never proved that. That was never proven."
jokes.setup: They need data on whether the fall height is fatal; Dennis suggests using a previous case
jokes.punchline: The 'previous case' is a woman who died after Dennis pushed her off a building — which he denies with practiced legal precision ('never proven')
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes and peak Dennis character comedy. Using his probable murder victim as a scientific data point, then immediately switching to 'never proven' legal defensive language, is pitch-perfect Dennis Reynolds. The escalation from 'we need data' to 'my murder victim' is excellent structure. Character integration is as high as it gets — only Dennis can make this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He's hardly a child, but he's still hanging on to his youth. That suggests daddy issues. His dad hates him as much as Mac's dad hates him.

jokes.text: "It was, I have to say, fortunate that she landed on her head, you know. Or at least he certainly made it look that way."
jokes.setup: Dennis insists he didn't push Maureen Ponderosa
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie's casual comments about the fall staging imply premeditated murder as background knowledge they've simply never raised before
jokes.explanation: 'Or at least he certainly made it look that way' is a great line — casual, matter-of-fact acknowledgment that the murder was staged. The nonchalance is the dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: My dad loves me. My name's an homage.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's an homage to a hamburger clown.

jokes.text: "Just go through their trash." / "Sleep with them." / "Talk to their priest, then sleep with their priest. Then blackmail the priest. Then go back to the priest and ask him to ask God to forgive you for blackmailing him."
jokes.setup: Dennis asks 'how do you truly get to know someone?' as a rhetorical setup for his social media plan
jokes.punchline: The group answers earnestly with an escalating series of increasingly unhinged methodologies, topped by Mac's priest-blackmail-forgiveness spiral
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation joke. Each answer reveals volumes about the character giving it: Charlie (surveillance-based), Dee (seduction), Mac (elaborate Catholic guilt spiral that becomes its own narrative). Mac's answer in particular — blackmail then ask forgiveness for the blackmail — is a compact, funny story that perfectly captures his religious self-loathing. The escalation structure is well-executed. Very quotable, strong character integration across all three.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Butt-eating... Where are you getting that from?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's a certain glint in the eye, you know, a sparkle.

jokes.text: "Lot, lot of pictures of food." / "I love that." / "Oh, I love that." / "Don't you love that? 'Cause I know what I ate. I don't know... I want to know what you ate. It's a good reminder that food is a thing."
jokes.setup: They're scrolling through Bryan O'Brien's social media to understand his state of mind
jokes.punchline: The group gets genuinely sidetracked enthusing about food photos, with Charlie's 'it's a good reminder that food is a thing' being a perfect non-insight
jokes.explanation: 'It's a good reminder that food is a thing' is a brilliantly vacant observation — Charlie expressing genuine gratitude for being reminded of the existence of food. The group's distraction from a suicide investigation to food-photo appreciation is good character comedy and observational social media satire.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You can see that in someone's eye?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Have you been eating butts? Of course she has!

jokes.text: Dennis's social media profile-reading spirals into diagnosing Bryan O'Brien with 'daddy issues' based on baseball cap orientation and tucked-in shirts
jokes.setup: Dennis claims they need to 'dig deeper' into the social media profile
jokes.punchline: His analytical framework is a parody of armchair psychology — hat style and shirt-tucking as reliable indicators of childhood trauma
jokes.explanation: Good Dennis character comedy. His false confidence in junk-science psychological profiling is on-brand and satirizes the kind of superficial social media analysis people actually do.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That Dee's a nasty fucking slut.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Definitely, definitely, but also that the poorly named Bryan O'Brien most definitely would kill himself.

jokes.text: "Plus, he gave him a comical name, like Mac's dad did. His dad hates him as much as Mac's dad hates him." / "No, my dad loves me. That... No, my name's an homage." / "It's an homage to a hamburger clown."
jokes.setup: Dennis connects Bryan O'Brien's ridiculous name to evidence of a bad father-son relationship
jokes.punchline: He draws the explicit parallel to Mac's name, and Mac's pathetic defense ('it's an homage') is immediately deflated — 'to a hamburger clown'
jokes.explanation: Strong callback payoff. Mac's delusional defense ('it's an homage') and Dennis's immediate correction ('to a hamburger clown') is a perfect two-step. The parallel between Bryan O'Brien and Mac Ronald McDonald is a genuinely good structural joke connecting the A-plot to character history.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah, he's a real deranged person. This kid's a real whack job. I'm afraid he's gonna do something really stupid this time.

jokes.text: "...and she introduced him to a whole new way of life: parasailing, Chilean wines, a tattoo of Spider-Man. Butt-eating..."
jokes.setup: Dennis is narrating Bryan O'Brien's romantic backstory with increasing specificity
jokes.punchline: The list of adventurous activities escalates plausibly — parasailing, wine, tattoo — then 'butt-eating' arrives as a sudden tonal left turn
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection/list structure. 'Parasailing, Chilean wines, a tattoo of Spider-Man' — each item makes the next feel possible, so when 'butt-eating' arrives it's genuinely surprising despite being a simple escalation. The Spider-Man tattoo is also funny on its own as an incongruous detail. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: My son is actually a big fan of yours. It would really get under his skin if he knew I was standing next to those. You. You.

jokes.text: "Butt-eating? Where are you getting that from?" / "Well... there's a certain glint in the eye, you know, a sparkle."
jokes.setup: Mac challenges Dennis's claim about butt-eating based on a photo
jokes.punchline: Dennis claims he can identify butt-eating proclivities from someone's eye contact in a photo — with complete, unshakeable confidence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Dennis moments. 'A certain glint in the eye, a sparkle' as his method for detecting sexual preferences from a photograph is both deeply creepy and brilliantly confident. This is peak Dennis Reynolds — his certainty is total, his methodology is insane. High originality because the joke is completely specific to him.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: We could become like a hot spot for jumpers. Turn them into martyrs. Highway to Hell, Free Fallin'.

jokes.text: "You can see that in someone's eye?" / "Oh, Dee." / "I'm asking." / "Have you been eating butts?" / "Of course she has! Nasty!"
jokes.setup: Dee asks a genuine clarifying question about whether butt-eating preferences show in the eyes
jokes.punchline: The group immediately interprets her intellectual curiosity as a confession of her own butt-eating activities
jokes.explanation: Good running extension of the Dee-as-scapegoat dynamic. 'Of course she has! Nasty!' is a funny line in context. The joke runs slightly long with everyone piling on, but the structure of her genuine question being read as a confession is solid.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The algorithm is telling us that this guy could die, wants to die, and that we should help him do it. That's just math.

jokes.text: "...and because of the copious requests for butt-eating, which, she was thinking was more of a one-time thing, and he was thinking, this is a thing now, like, from now on."
jokes.setup: Dennis narrates the girlfriend's breakup reasoning
jokes.punchline: The 'one-time thing vs. ongoing expectation' framing of the butt-eating dispute is treated as a completely relatable relationship misalignment
jokes.explanation: The joke works because the 'she thought it was a one-time thing' framing is exactly how people discuss mundane relationship miscommunications — applied to something completely absurd. Dennis's confidence in this analysis is funny. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Feelings just get in the way.

jokes.text: "That Dee's a nasty fucking slut." — stated as the primary algorithmic conclusion of their research session
jokes.setup: Dennis asks 'algorithm-wise, what have we learned today?'
jokes.punchline: Mac's summary of their social media research is entirely about Dee, not Bryan O'Brien — their investigation has been hijacked by their need to shame their friend
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — the 'summary' of their algorithm session being entirely about shaming Dee rather than the task at hand is the punchline. The deadpan delivery as a data conclusion ('algorithm-wise') gives it extra lift.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: I'll push him. I don't give a shit.

jokes.text: "Baby, I'll do anything you want. My son is actually a big fan of yours. I mean, it would really get under his skin if he knew I was standing next to those. Uh, you. You."
jokes.setup: News reporter Jackie Denardo approaches Frank claiming to want to interview him as the concerned father
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately tries to pick up the reporter, admits he's motivated by spite toward his son, then catches himself objectifying her mid-sentence and self-corrects to 'you'
jokes.explanation: 'Those. Uh, you. You.' is a great character beat — Frank can't complete a respectful sentence. His transparent motivations (flirting, spite) wrapped in paternal concern framing is good Frank character work.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: If I want to bang it, I'm gonna bang it. Not that I am banging it, but I could. And if it doesn't splatter to bits, I'm gonna bang it later.

jokes.text: "Yeah, kind of grim. I'd probably take my business elsewhere." / "You don't have business."
jokes.setup: The gang discusses whether being known as a 'suicide bar' would hurt business
jokes.punchline: Cricket weighs in as a consumer; Mac immediately points out Cricket has no business to take anywhere
jokes.explanation: Quick, economical Cricket joke. 'You don't have business' is the right length response. Gets a bit repetitive as it's used twice with Cricket ('You don't have business, Cricket' / 'You don't have business, guy').

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: He's calling me strange?

jokes.text: "'Highway to Hell.' 'Free Fallin'.' 'Free Fallin'.' Come on, man."
jokes.setup: They're planning the music for their suicide-themed bar
jokes.punchline: 'Free Fallin'' as a song choice for a bar that hosts people jumping from the roof — obvious but embraced with such genuine enthusiasm it works
jokes.explanation: Decent bit. 'Free Fallin'' is an obvious enough choice that the joke is partly in Dennis's enthusiasm ('Come on, man'). Not particularly original but fits the sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Let's try to think of it more analytically, more mathematically. It's sort of like a deletion. Like hitting Control-Alt-Delete. Bloop. He's in the trash.

jokes.text: "The algorithm is telling us, mathematically, scientifically, that this guy could die, wants to die, and that we should help him do it. That's just math."
jokes.setup: Dennis is walking through the algorithmic conclusion logically
jokes.punchline: The algorithm, designed to remove emotion from decision-making, has arrived at a recommendation to commit murder — 'that's just math' as the final justification
jokes.explanation: The thematic centerpiece of the episode and one of its best jokes. The payoff of the algorithm satire is that the removal of human emotion from decision-making leads to a logical conclusion to commit murder — with 'that's just math' as a chillingly casual button. This is the episode's thesis statement delivered as a punchline. It's funny AND satirically sharp AND character-specific to Dennis. The best single joke in the episode by a margin.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: What a gyp. We were gonna... we had a good plan.

jokes.text: "Well, it still feels a little weird, but feelings are irrelevant in the face of facts." / "Yeah." / "Is that what I'm hearing? The feelings... feelings just get in the way."
jokes.setup: The algorithm has concluded they should help the man die
jokes.punchline: The characters rationalize away their own moral instincts using the episode's established anti-feeling framework — feelings are 'irrelevant,' 'in the way'
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the satirical moment. Charlie's hesitation ('still feels a little weird') is the last flicker of humanity before it's suppressed by the algorithm logic. The group enthusiastically agreeing that feelings are the enemy is a sharp satirical beat.

dialogue.speaker: Bryan
dialogue.line: This isn't my dad.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Not of this sad sack. I got distracted by the reporter's bagonzas.

jokes.text: "Yeah. I'll push him off the building. I don't give a shit."
jokes.setup: They're trying to figure out the best way to 'help' the man die per the algorithm
jokes.punchline: Mac volunteers to push him with total nonchalance — no planning, no moral qualm, just immediate practical volunteering for murder
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy joke. 'I'll push him off the building. I don't give a shit.' delivered as a mundane logistical offer — like offering to pick up dry cleaning — is perfect Mac characterization and peak dark comedy. Five seconds, maximum impact.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's where I stash my Maui Kush.

jokes.text: Frank's on-camera interview to the news reporter is entirely about his casaba melon: 'If I want to bang it, I'm gonna bang it. Not that I am banging it, but I could. And if it doesn't splatter to bits, I'm gonna bang it later. Because it's my property.'
jokes.setup: Frank is being interviewed as the concerned father of the suicidal man; reporter asks if he wants to say anything to his son
jokes.punchline: Frank's televised message to his 'son' is entirely a property-rights defense of his right to have sex with a melon — accidentally broadcast to the city
jokes.explanation: Great payoff for the melon subplot. The juxtaposition of the emotional father-son TV moment with Frank's property-rights rant about melon sex is excellent. 'Not that I am banging it, but I could' is a beautiful legalistic non-denial. The accidental public broadcast elevates the absurdity. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Pot's pretty much legal now. You don't really have to stash it anywhere.

jokes.text: "Okay, Cricket, uh, here's a broom. You probably sneak up there, give him a little nudge, and, uh, you know, don't let anyone see you commit the murder."
jokes.setup: News breaks that the jumper is coming down voluntarily, so they need someone to push him before he does
jokes.punchline: Dennis assigns Cricket the murder as a quick errand, hands him a broom, and adds the afterthought 'don't let anyone see you commit the murder' — using the word 'murder' casually
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy beat. The broom as the murder weapon of choice and 'don't let anyone see you commit the murder' as an afterthought are both funny. Using Cricket as the designated murder-errand-runner is consistent with his series role.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I wouldn't eat it, Cricks. It's full of loads.

jokes.text: "Guys, can-can we just not call it a murder? Let's try to think of it more analytically, more mathematically. It's sort of like a deletion. You know? Like hitting Control-Alt-Delete. Bloop. He's in the trash."
jokes.setup: Cricket hesitates at the word 'murder'
jokes.punchline: Dennis reframes murder as a computer deletion process — 'Control-Alt-Delete. Bloop. He's in the trash.' — with cheerful confidence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's two or three best jokes. Dennis applying computer UI language to murder — 'Control-Alt-Delete, Bloop, He's in the trash' — is both a perfect satire of tech-bro dehumanization and genuinely funny on its own terms. It's the episode's algorithm metaphor taken to its logical extreme. The word 'bloop' is inspired. High originality, exceptional character integration (only Dennis speaks this way), excellent economy. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mathematically we were supposed to kill a man today. Maybe that's part of the problem of taking the humanity out of decisions.

jokes.text: "G... oh, dude, that's... What a gyp. Yeah. We were gonna... we had a good plan."
jokes.setup: News breaks that the jumper is coming down alive and not jumping
jokes.punchline: The gang's reaction to the man NOT dying is disappointment that their murder plan is foiled
jokes.explanation: 'We had a good plan' as a lament for a foiled murder scheme is good dark comedy. The characterization of the man's survival as a 'gyp' for the audience (the gang) is appropriately awful.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's full of loads.

jokes.text: "Can I say something, though? I think this is for the best." / "That's not the algorithm..." / "Like, we were going down a road I was not totally comfortable with."
jokes.setup: The gang is disappointed the man survived
jokes.punchline: Mac's belated moral awakening — 'I was not totally comfortable' — after he volunteered to push the man off a building moments ago is a perfect character beat in cowardly self-revision
jokes.explanation: Good character beat. Mac's retroactive discomfort after volunteering for murder is classic IASIP revisionism — the characters back away from consequences while pretending they were always ambivalent.

jokes.text: "You guys want to go back to watching our show?" — the gang immediately pivots back to their British period drama after nearly orchestrating a murder
jokes.setup: The crisis is resolved; the gang is processing what just happened
jokes.punchline: Dee's immediate pivot back to television watching — without any reflection on nearly having a man murdered — treats the near-murder as equivalent to a minor TV interruption
jokes.explanation: Good structural callback. The episode ends where it began — watching TV — with the implication that nothing has changed and nothing was learned. The speed of the pivot back to entertainment is the dark punchline.

jokes.text: "This isn't my dad. That's not Dennis." / "I thought you said you were the dad." / "Not of this sad sack."
jokes.setup: An emotional father-son reunion is set up; Bryan O'Brien comes down expecting his estranged father
jokes.punchline: Frank is not his father — he is a random old man who lied to get close to the news reporter — and Frank dismisses the man as a 'sad sack' with zero empathy
jokes.explanation: 'Not of this sad sack' is a perfectly Frank line. The emotional manipulation of the entire situation — Frank posing as a concerned father to hit on a reporter — is revealed cleanly. Good structural payoff.

jokes.text: The 'father' reunites with 'son' — neither is related to the other; Frank was just distracted by the reporter's body. 'I got distracted by the reporter's bagonzas.'
jokes.setup: An emotional father-son reunion is about to happen on live TV
jokes.punchline: The 'father' is not related to the jumper at all — Frank lied to get inside; the reason he was at the scene was entirely about the reporter's breasts ('bagonzas')
jokes.explanation: Solid payoff to the Frank-as-father setup. 'Bagonzas' is a great Frank word. The deflation of the emotional reunion (which was always fake) is a perfect Frank moment. 'Speaking of melons, there's a casaba with my name on it in there' is a great immediate pivot.

jokes.text: "I got distracted by the reporter's bagonzas." — Frank's explanation for the mix-up
jokes.setup: Frank is asked why he pretended to be the man's father
jokes.punchline: 'Bagonzas' as Frank's invented/personal slang for breasts, delivered as a completely reasonable explanation for orchestrating a fake emotional moment
jokes.explanation: 'Bagonzas' is a genuinely funny invented word — it sounds exactly like something Frank would say, is entirely specific to him, and is delivered as if it's self-explanatory. High character integration. The casualness of the explanation after ruining a man's potential reconciliation with his real father is good dark comedy.

jokes.text: "Speaking of melons, there's a casaba with my name on it in there."
jokes.setup: Frank has just mentioned 'bagonzas'
jokes.punchline: Frank segues from breasts ('bagonzas') to 'melons' back to his casaba — a chain of wordplay that happens to also remind everyone of his sexual melon relationship
jokes.explanation: Nice wordplay callback. Frank's 'speaking of melons' connecting bagonzas to casaba is a sly double-entendre chain that keeps the melon joke alive efficiently.

jokes.text: "Oh... Ah... Oh, God. Ugh!" — collective reaction to Frank revealing the casaba has a hole in it
jokes.setup: Frank opens the casaba melon to reveal what's inside; the group sees it
jokes.punchline: Their cascade of disgusted noises confirms the sexual-use suspicion the audience has held for ten minutes — a visual gag payoff that the transcript captures through pure reaction
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat is the punchline — the audience fills in what the characters are seeing. The long buildup to this payoff has been patient and the visual disgust response (imagined through the transcript) is the right delivery mechanism. Good structural patience.

jokes.text: "It's where I stash my Maui Kush." — Frank's actual reason for the secret casaba melon
jokes.setup: The group has assumed for the entire episode that Frank is having sex with the melon
jokes.punchline: The reveal is that it's just a weed stash — the entire sexual deviance subplot was a red herring; Frank is just a drug-stashing paranoid, not a melon-fucker
jokes.explanation: The best structural joke in the episode. The reveal works because it's both completely unexpected and completely logical — Frank would absolutely hide his weed in a melon and guard it obsessively. The episode spent ten minutes building the audience's certainty that this was a sex-with-melon situation, then pulled the rug. This is excellent misdirection. The rewatch bonus is high because the second viewing completely recontextualizes all of Frank's protective behavior. 'Maui Kush' as the specific strain named is a nice extra touch.

jokes.text: "Pot's pretty much legal now. You don't really have to stash it anywhere." / "When did that happen?"
jokes.setup: Frank reveals his elaborate melon stash system for hiding marijuana
jokes.punchline: Mac points out weed is basically legal now, making Frank's entire system pointless; Frank is genuinely unaware of this
jokes.explanation: 'When did that happen?' is a great Frank line — his criminal paranoia is so deep he missed a decade of drug policy reform. Good character beat that extends the reveal's comedic value.

jokes.text: "What? You're still watching that British show? I mean, that's a bunch of crap. It stinks." — Frank's instant verdict after the algorithm endorsed it
jokes.setup: The gang has been watching the show because the algorithm says they like it
jokes.punchline: Frank, who wasn't subjected to the algorithm, has an unfiltered opinion — it's crap — which triggers an admission from the others that they also don't actually like it
jokes.explanation: Good beat that opens up the episode's thematic resolution. Frank as the truth-teller who isn't algorithmically compromised is a nice structural function. His blunt verdict unlocks the others' suppressed honest opinions.

jokes.text: "I hate the plot because it's absurd. The plot is ridiculous. Right? The scullery maid?" / "And their teeth, I find them hard to look at." / "The teeth are a little bit of a mess, but mathematically we're supposed to like the show."
jokes.setup: Frank's criticism unlocks everyone's honest opinions about the British show
jokes.punchline: Dennis acknowledges the show has obvious problems but defers to 'mathematically' — still unable to override the algorithm even when confronted with his own dislike
jokes.explanation: Strong thematic payoff. Dennis saying 'the teeth are a little bit of a mess, but mathematically we're supposed to like the show' is the satirical thesis perfectly articulated — people deferring to algorithmic recommendations over their own direct experience. This is the episode's moral, delivered as character comedy.

jokes.text: "Uh, yeah, I know, but mathematically we were supposed to kill a man today. Maybe that's, like, part of the problem of, like, taking the humanity out of decisions. Perhaps the science just isn't there yet."
jokes.setup: Dennis defends the algorithm for TV recommendations despite everyone admitting they don't like the show
jokes.punchline: Charlie's summary of the episode's moral — 'we were supposed to kill a man today' — delivered as an abstract philosophical observation with 'perhaps the science just isn't there yet' as a mealy-mouthed hedge
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and its thematic capstone. Charlie articulating 'maybe taking humanity out of decisions is a problem' using the murder attempt as the supporting example, then concluding with 'perhaps the science just isn't there yet' — as if this is a minor technical setback rather than a moral catastrophe — is excellent character comedy and satirical writing. The hedge 'perhaps the science just isn't there yet' is brilliantly wrong-headed. High quotability.

jokes.text: "I wouldn't eat it, Cricks. It's full of loads."
jokes.setup: Cricket is about to eat the casaba melon after finding out it's just a weed stash
jokes.punchline: Dennis warns Cricket it's 'full of loads' — implying the melon WAS used sexually despite Frank's explanation, or that Frank's marijuana use left behind something unsavory
jokes.explanation: Perfect episode-closing joke. After the misdirect reveal (it's just weed), Dennis drops 'it's full of loads' as the last word — which either means Frank was lying, or that the weed stash somehow accumulated additional material. Either reading is funny. It undoes the clean resolution of the melon mystery and sends the audience out laughing. Economy is exceptional — four words close out a ten-minute subplot. The word 'loads' is specifically funny.

tmdb_overview: Trapped inside Paddy's with a suicide jumper on the roof, the Gang wonders if they should bother intervening with an algorithm of their own - Could he, would he, should we? the second half hour, Dennis and Charlie stand guard at the entrance to their laser tag base waiting to ambush the legendary "Big Mo," but Dennis begins to ponder the reasons they play laser tag and if their pursuit of a victory is worth their effort.
